idiom_name: with statement over context managers (__enter__/__exit__), @contextlib.contextmanager and ExitStack for the compact forms
implementation_notes: The with statement is the language's RAII form: __enter__ runs first and establishes the invariant, __exit__ runs on every exit path - normal return, break/continue, exception - and a truthy return from __exit__ suppresses the exception, so the classic owner class is replaced by those two protocol methods or by one generator wrapped with @contextlib.contextmanager. contextlib.ExitStack composes a dynamic number of resources (including conditionally acquired ones) with LIFO release, and async with/AsyncExitStack do the same for async resources. Finalizers are not a release point: CPython frees reference-counted objects promptly, but __del__ is unreliable under cycles, on other implementations and at interpreter shutdown, which is why weakref.finalize exists as a safety net and the documentation steers to context managers.
pitfalls: In a @contextlib.contextmanager generator the code after yield is skipped when an exception leaves the with block unless it sits in try/finally: the exception is thrown into the generator at the yield, so a bare yield leaks on the exceptional path.

Relying on __del__ (or on dropping the last reference) for release is non-deterministic under reference cycles, on non-CPython implementations and at interpreter shutdown; with, contextlib and weakref.finalize are the supported forms.

An ExitStack holds everything it ever registered until it unwinds and releases LIFO, so a stack that lives longer than the function (or a resource registered after an early exit) keeps handles past their usefulness.
